content_html_sanitized:
The headline was chosen to demonstrate the relevance to cannabis. But let me make clear that I have no hesitation about saying that there is no scientific basis for psychiatry as a medical practice.

 

Recently, there was a widely reported news story about a surgeon removing a patient’s liver instead of his spleen. Oops. The patient died, but there was no debate about whether there is a difference between a liver and a spleen.

 

Now, consider that there are three major “schools” in psychiatry, Freudian, Adlerian, and Jungian. In addition there are two more psychiatrists that I particularly like, Victor Frankl and Thomas Szasz.

 

Szasz is of particular relevance because he argues that there is no such thing as “mental illness.” That really is “off topic” for MarijuanaNews, but his views about the politicization of psychiatry are very much on topic.  

In June of 2000, he was interviewed for Reason Magazine,

Curing the Therapeutic State: Thomas Szasz interviewed by Jacob Sullum. Thomas Szasz on the medicalization of American life.

 

Jacob is an old friend, who worked for NORML when I was National Director, and is truly one of the smartest people I have had the privilege of knowing. I strongly recommend this interview.

 

If psychiatrists as psychiatrists did not claim special expertise in recommending cannabis policies, none of this would be relevant for MarijuanaNews. In the real world, psychiatrists do not have any relevant expertise on economics, criminal law, or public health regulations, such as DEA drug schedules, the things relevant to cannabis policy.

 

Moreover, they do not have any expertise on cannabis per se. If Psychiatry was a perfect analysis of the human mind, it would still not be authoritative on social issues, such as economics, or criminal justice.

See Appeal to False Authority

 

Here is an example of a very policized psychiatrist, Mark Gold, offering a supposedly authoritative opinion on the medical efficacy of cannabis in areas where he has no special knowledge.

See

Is Cannabis Medicine?

Purchasers seem to think so but new research says not so fast.

Excerpt: “For example, there are no psychiatric indications approved by the FDA for cannabinoids, and limited evidence supporting the therapeutic use of cannabinoids for psychiatric disorders. The current evidence is insufficient to support prescribing cannabinoids for the treatment of psychiatric disorders. To date, evidence supporting cannabinoid prescription beyond FDA indications is strongest for the management of chronic pain and spasticity.

There is clear evidence that cannabinoids have potential for harm, especially in vulnerable populations such as adolescents and those at risk of psychotic disorders.”

 

Now consider the real world record of psychiatry and specifically its relation to prescription drug use. It is promiscuous with everything except cannabis.
